rv.q: Smith is certainly not a good man for the job. But this is the only high school in a one-stoplight town in Appalachian Georgia, so he’ll have to do. His actual job is to teach his students “The Crucible,” a rite of passage for almost all American schoolchildren.
John The Villain reclaims their souls, as the girls in Mr. Smith’s class speak the truth once and for all and at long last.
Belflower's play hits as hard as it does because at its heart, fighting their way through one hell of a junior year, are the kind of heroes we actually need.
Taymor's production is entirely sympathetic - to the characters and to the text.
Belflower has written the most energizing and emotionally wrecking drama this season, an unsentimental education for teens screaming to stay sane in a fucked society.
It’s a testament to the subtle brilliance of Kimberly Belflower’s writing and Danya Tamor’s direction that you can hardly feel the 105-minute, no-intermission runtime of John Proctor Is the Villain.
John Proctor Is the Villain doesn't feel like a show designed to goose youth-audience ticket sales; it feels like one that will engage and electrify a teenage audience, and plenty of adults too.
Belflower’s first Broadway play is a galvanizing accomplishment all on its own.
Daring and spirited performances from the actors elevate the material above the level of curriculum.
I wish “John Proctor” made its very fair point about girls forging their own narratives with more ambivalence and less certitude, especially in its less-than-credible last few minutes
But while “John Proctor” is a good time, it is not a powerful one.
Belflower is a master of teen-speak.
Consider this your green light and dance your way to the ASAP.

Smart and sensitive, funny and harrowing, thoughtful and explosive in its exploration of the inner lives of teenage girls, John Proctor Is the Villain is an American classic in the making like The Crucible before it.
The cast and director Danya Taymor craft a simmering stage of very teenage drama, humor, friendships, alliances, gossip, resentments, and ultimately collective power.

In a cultural climate where diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are under attack—and where critical engagement with race, gender, and power is being labeled “divisive”—this play feels not just timely but necessary.
John Proctor Is the Villain is truly a most engaging play, with a terrific ensemble cast that makes even discussions about The Crucible thoroughly engrossing.
Exactly the kind of funny, pointed, contemporary comic drama that Broadway can use more of.
John Proctor Is the Villain is much like that: a heady rush of glee, shock and understanding that takes you by surprise, and leaves you happy you came.

Under Danya Taymor’s fast-paced, nicely articulated staging, the cast, whose high schoolers, as usual, are played by slightly older actors, is funny and energetic, with uniformly quality performances.

Whatever your take on “The Crucible,” #MeToo, or any of the ongoing debates concerning women’s roles and responsibilities, to themselves and others, you’ll likely leave the theater feeling more bewitched than bothered.

Opening at the start of Spring Break, “John Proctor is the Villain” is an entertainment that doubles as an appropriate lesson for teenagers in history and literature, and for their parents in popular culture.
It’s meaningful, silly, powerful, extremely high school, and worth the price of admission.
That’s exactly how you’ll feel after enduring this well-meaning but exhausting play.
Ebert delivers this production’s only compelling performance, and when he leaves the stage, I could only wait for his theatrical toxicity to return to give me something to watch.

While Belflower’s play is clever and insightful, it is also contrived and manipulative, attempting to shoehorn almost every feminist hot button topic into one story overlaying The Crucible: date rape, sexual abuse, sexual harassment on the job, toxic masculinity, patriarch dominance.

This was my near-breathless reaction to experiencing the first half of Kimberly Belflower's absolutely riveting and thought-provoking new play, John Proctor Is the Villain, the second most electrifying and manipulative production I have seen this season.
Teenagers should see this play and study it alongside Miller’s.
Belflower's remarkable play is more than just a riff on Arthur Miller.
Under Danya Taymor’s meticulous direction, the cast of “John Proctor” define the meaning of liberation in an exquisite fashion.
John Proctor is the Villain is a beautiful show with the moving ending.
There is a rawness and authenticity to this show like no other, and it will certainly spark conversations with viewers, and it will stick with them, long after it is over.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this #MeToo-era rethinking of "The Crucible" as smart and timely, praising Belflower's sharp writing and the youthful energy. Some find it occasionally heavy-handed or underdeveloped, but most laud its provocative feminist perspective.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.

vr.q: It is one of my favorite things I've seen all year, actually... I would encourage you to go and check this out as soon as possible on Broadway because if you're anything like me, you're going to want to go and see it a second time. It is that good.
It's rare to see such strong writing, directing, and performances all in perfect alignment with one another. I apologize to everyone's wallets, but I think this is another must-see.
I loved this play. I really, really enjoyed it.
There are many reasons why I shouldn't like Kimberly Belflower's play, John Proctor is the Villain, and yet I loved it.
It's a coming of age play about reclaiming your story and the deep healing power of friendship...I laughed a lot, and I cried even more.
John Proctor is the villain is one of my favorite shows on Broadway right now. It's my pick for best play at the Tony Awards.
